Breadboard

Design system for the Kiki bilingual (Odia–English) learning app · offline copy built 2026-10-12 from design-system/project/ · last change: Mastery colours changed: green = concept, red = words, yellow = English, blue = lab (practical). README, tokens usage, bundle, component guides and all Kiki guide artwork updated; Kiki's four dots keep Google order.

Breadboard is the design system for a bilingual Odia–English learning app for first-year engineering students. The app looks like a friendly electronics breadboard on graph paper, and Google's four colours appear only when the student earns them. A new student sees ink on paper with one spot of colour, Kiki's four dots. A student near mid-sem sees a map lit up in green, red, yellow and blue.

Content fundamentals

  • Write short, plain sentences. Kiki speaks at most two sentences at a time.
  • Address the student as "you". Kiki says "I". Use sentence case everywhere. No emoji, no exclamation marks except in a celebration ("Spot on!").
  • Keep every English technical term in English, in a TermChip, at every dial level. Never translate the term itself; explain it in Odia in the term's sheet. Example: "forward biasରେ, ପ୍ରାୟ 0.7 V ର cut-in voltage ପରେ ଏହା current ପ୍ରବାହିତ କରେ।"
  • Name what went wrong as "not yet", never "wrong". A language gap gets this sentence: "You understand this. You just need the English words."
  • Buttons state the action: "Start lesson", "Run simulation", "Practise the words".
  • The Odia sample copy in these components is placeholder text. A native speaker must review it before the demo.

Colour

Colour is earned. Brand colour marks mastery and Kiki; everything else is ink, pencil and line on paper and paper-raised.

DimensionFill tokenText tokenMeans
Conceptgreengreen-ink"I understand it"
Wordsredred-ink"I know what it's called"
Englishyellowyellow-ink"I can explain it in English"
Lab (practical)blueblue-ink"I can make it work"
  • Always show the four dimensions in this order: concept, words, English, lab, which is green, red, yellow, blue (ring segments clockwise from the top, progress segments). Kiki's four dots keep Google's order (blue, red, yellow, green): they are Kiki's identity, not a progress readout. When Kiki leads with a dimension, the dot of that colour grows.
  • Use the fill tokens for shapes only. For text and icons use the -ink tokens, which meet 4.5:1 on paper and paper-raised in both themes. Never set text in yellow on paper. Text on a yellow fill is on-yellow.
  • red never means wrong; it means Words. green never means correct on its own; it means Concept. Correct answers always carry a tick and a word as well as colour. A wrong answer is a dashed pencil outline. A correct answer lights up in the colour of the dimension being practised.
  • An owned term chip or sticker uses a red-strong fill with white text.
  • The primary button fill is blue-ink with on-blue-ink text, because blue with white text is below 4.5:1.
  • Lab mode is a scope: scope-glass background, scope-grid lines, scope-trace for output, blue for the student's prediction, scope-text for readouts.
  • Use tints (blue-tint, red-tint, yellow-tint, green-tint) for quiet grounds behind notes, never as the only signal.

Type

  • Headings: display-l and display-m (Baloo 2). Odia headings: odia-display-m (Baloo Bhaina 2, the same family), set 2px larger with a looser line height.
  • Running text: body (Noto Sans) for English and body-odia (Noto Sans Oriya) for Odia and mixed sentences. Odia glyphs read smaller and need room for vowel marks, so Odia runs are 12% larger with a 1.66 line height; MorphText does this automatically.
  • English terms: term. Labels and pills: label. Values and units: mono (Roboto Mono) with tabular figures.
  • hand (Kalam) appears only inside Snap your answer mock-ups.
  • All fonts load from Google Fonts; components/bundle.css imports them.

Space, shape and the breadboard

  • Spacing steps: space-1 to space-8. space-2 (8px) is also the breadboard grid: the .bb-grid-bg class draws grid-dot dots every 8px behind pages.
  • Corners: radius-node for map nodes, radius-card for cards and stickers, radius-sheet for bottom sheets, radius-pill for buttons, chips and the dial.
  • Buttons and stickers sit on a key edge (key-edge-blue, key-edge-neutral) and press down 2px on tap. Use lift only for popovers and sheets.
  • The metaphor carries the interface: concepts are components, prerequisites are wires, mastering a concept lights its LED and sends current down the wire, loading is a pulse of current, an error is a broken wire with Kiki's dots drifting apart.

Motion, sound and haptics

  • Tap feedback 120 ms, small changes 250 ms on a spring, screen changes 350 ms, celebrations at most 1.2 s. Current flow is a dashed line moving along a wire.
  • With reduced motion on, every animation stops and changes are instant.
  • Five sounds only: tap tick, sticker pop, a rising three-note chime, a power-on hum for a mastered concept, and Kiki's voice, which always waits for a tap.
  • Android haptics: 10 ms per dial notch, 30 ms on a correct answer.

Focus and accessibility

  • Keyboard focus is a 2px solid focus-ring outline with a 2px offset on every interactive component.
  • The dial is a slider (arrow keys, Home, End). Rings, scopes and charts carry text labels. Status colours always come with a word ("not yet", "language gap").
  • The class pulse hides any concept with fewer than 10 students.

Iconography

Use Material Symbols Rounded (loaded from Google Fonts in bundle.css). Outlined icons switch to filled when something is earned. No emoji, no other icon sets. Kiki is the only character. Kiki has two forms and no other features: the four dots (Kiki) and the pointer (KikiPointer), a cursor with two eyes. Never add a mouth, limbs or a full face. Static artwork for every pointer state is in the Kiki asset group.

How Kiki guides

  • Kiki uses two forms. The four dots are for presence: the avatar, the caption bar, loading. The pointer is for guidance: whenever Kiki points at, demonstrates or watches something on screen. The student's own cursor or finger is never replaced.
  • In a lesson, Kiki explains through KikiWalkthrough: a dark caption bar plays one sentence at a time (Odia first, English under it) while the pointer moves to the word or diagram part that sentence is about.
  • Kiki marks a word in one of five ways, always in the colour of the skill being taught: sweep (an underline draws under the word as it is said), marker (a highlighter stroke behind the word while the rest of the paragraph dims), lens (a card opens with the word at 28px, its Odia meaning and Hear it), connect (a dashed line from the word to the matching point on the diagram) and circle (a hand-drawn loop for exam vocabulary). Technical words are red, ideas green, exam English yellow, lab controls blue.
  • Words are never enlarged in place, so text never reflows. Only the lens zooms.
  • In the lab, Kiki follows LabGuide: show me once with a ghost drag, wait at the part for the student's turn, tilt and explain in one sentence after a wrong move, dim everything but the next control and tap it, then ask "why" at the output. The callout is always attached to the pointer.

Components

Load React 18, then components/bundle.css and components/bundle.js; everything is on window.Breadboard. Build screens only from these components; add a component here before it appears on a screen.

  • Actions: Button.
  • Kiki: Kiki (nine states).
  • Language: LanguageDial, MorphText, TermChip, WordSticker.
  • Progress: MasteryRing, LessonProgress, ReceiptCompare, MapNode.
  • Learning: DiodeExplorable (the template for every explorable), DiagnosisCard, VoiceScope.
  • Lab: PredictionCanvas, LabStepper, Spotlight, FaultCard.
  • Exam: AnswerOverlay (Snap your answer), PracticeReport (analysis of a written practice set), and MapNode in the repair state for the weak-spot repair map.
  • Feedback: Snackbar, SourceTag.
  • Teachers: ClassPulseBar.
  • Guidance: KikiPointer, KikiWalkthrough, LabGuide.

window.Breadboard.samples holds the worked example used in the previews: the diode lesson at all five dial levels, its glossary and a marked Snap answer.

Components

Live previews, running the same bundle.js the app uses (window.Breadboard, React 18). Switch the theme in the sidebar to see dark mode.

Actions

Button

Tactile keys: filled, tonal, text

A tactile pill key with a darker bottom edge that presses down 2px on tap; use one filled Button per screen for the main action.

Consumer provides: children (the label, a verb: "Start lesson", "Run simulation"), optional variant (filled default, tonal, text), optional icon (a Material Symbols Rounded name) and any native button props.

  • Do: one filled key per screen; tonal for secondary actions; text for links like "Show me the whole map".
  • Do: write the label as the action that happens.
  • Don't: put two filled keys side by side, or use red or green fills (those colours are mastery dimensions).

Kiki

Kiki

Nine states made from four dots

The helper character, drawn as four Google-coloured dots that rearrange to show what Kiki is doing.

Consumer provides: state (idle, listening, thinking, speaking, pointing, asking, celebrating, unsure, examiner), optional size (px, default 64), lead (concept | words | english | lab: that dimension's dot grows to show what is being practised), direction (degrees, for pointing), label (accessible name).

  • Do: dock Kiki bottom-right on the phone; float it beside the target in the lab.
  • Do: switch to unsure when screenshot reading is not confident, and offer the known-state picker.
  • Don't: give Kiki a face, speech bubbles longer than two sentences, or any colours beyond the four dots.

KikiPointer

Kiki's guide form: eleven states

Kiki's guide form: a rounded cursor with two eyes and the four coloured dots trailing behind it, used wherever Kiki points at, demonstrates or watches something on screen.

Consumer provides: state, optional size (px; 40 to 48 on top of lesson content, 46 to 56 in the lab, 72+ for teaching moments), lead (concept | words | english | lab: that dot grows and colours the tap ripple and wait ring), flip (mirror to point left), label, style.

Place it so the cursor tip, at (12, 8) in the 80 × 80 viewBox, sits on the target. KikiWalkthrough and LabGuide do this for you.

StateUse it when Kiki is…What moves
idlepresent but not actingbobs gently, blinks
pointingshowing where to looknudges toward the tip, dots tucked in
tappingasking the student to tap or click herepresses down; a ripple in the lead colour
draggingdemonstrating a dragtilts and carries a ghost part
tracingreading a word or line with the studenttilts and slides along the text
thinkingwaiting for Geminidots orbit the cursor
askingasking a "why" questioneyes look up, dots form a question mark
listeningrecording the student's voicedots become equaliser bars
celebratingmarking a successhops, happy eyes, dots burst
unsurenot confident about the screentilts, eyes look around, dots drift. Always pair with the known-state picker
waitingwaiting for the student at the next controlstill, with a turning dashed ring at the tip

Guiding like a companion cursor

Kiki behaves like a companion cursor: it lives beside the student's own cursor or finger, flies to the thing that matters, and shows the route instead of describing it. A state alone is a pose; guidance is a state plus these marks around it (see assets/Kiki/ for every move drawn on the series-or-parallel example):

MovePointer stateMarks around it
Look herepointingKiki flies in (dots trail its path); a halo and a filled step number land on the target
Path aheadpointing, eyes on the next stepSteps still to come appear as ghost numbers on a dashed route that flows towards them
TracetracingA rail beside the wire or text: solid behind Kiki, dashed ahead
ConnectpointingTwo targets haloed, joined by arrows, with what they share named
Your turnwaitingA turning dashed ring on the target; Kiki parks beside it, never on it
RedirectpointingA curved arrow from the student's tap to the right target. Copy says "Look here instead", never "wrong"
Show medraggingThe ghost part travels from the tray to the slot along the route
DonecelebratingThe whole route solid, every step ticked
  • Do: show at most three steps at once: the one now and the next two. Further steps appear as the student moves.
  • Do: let the eyes lead. Kiki looks at the next step before it moves there.
  • Do: run marks beside lines (a rail 8 px off), so the student's diagram stays readable under them.
  • Don't: park the pointer on top of the thing the student must tap or read.

Rules

  • Do: keep the body dark with its white outline in both themes. It sits over screenshots, scopes and paper alike, like a system cursor.
  • Do: keep the student's own cursor or finger separate. Kiki's pointer never replaces it.
  • Don't: give Kiki a mouth, arms or other expressions beyond the two eyes. Personality comes from posture, motion and the dots.
  • Don't: move the pointer while the student is dragging; wait, then react.

KikiWalkthrough

Kiki explains a lesson card, word by word

Kiki explains a lesson card: a caption bar plays the narration one sentence at a time while Kiki's pointer moves through the paragraph and the diagram, marking the word or idea each sentence is about.

Consumer provides: data ({paragraph, steps, figure?}): paragraph is strings plus {id, text, phrase?} targets; each step is {target, action, dim, odia, en, to?}. Optional autoPlay, stepMs (default 3800). Without data it plays the diode sample.

How Kiki marks a word. One action per narration sentence, in the colour of the skill being taught (dim):

ActionLooks likeUse for
sweepan underline draws itself left to right under the word as Kiki says itfirst mention of a term
markera highlighter stroke behind the word; the rest of the paragraph dims to 40%the one idea of this sentence
lensthe word is marked and a lens card opens below it: the word at 28px, its Odia meaning, Hear ita new or hard technical term
connectthe word is marked and a dashed line runs from it to the matching point on the diagram, which pulseslinking a word to the graph or circuit
circlea hand-drawn loop around the wordexam vocabulary or a word to say exactly

Colours: technical words red (Words), ideas and phrases green (Concept), exam English yellow (English), lab controls blue (Lab). Text is never enlarged in place, so the paragraph never reflows. Only the lens zooms.

  • Do: write one sentence per step, at most 18 words, Odia first with the English line under it, following the dial.
  • Do: let the student pause, step back and tap any word at any time; the walkthrough is a guide, not a video.
  • Don't: mark more than one target at once, or chain more than 8 steps on one card.

LabGuide

Kiki guiding inside the lab tool: show me, then your turn

Kiki inside a lab tool: it demonstrates the step once with a ghost drag, waits at the control for the student's turn, reacts to wrong moves, spotlights the next button and then asks "why" about the output.

The sequence for every lab step:

  1. Show me. The pointer flies to the part (pointing), carries a ghost copy to its place (dragging), then celebrates.
  2. Your turn. The pointer waits on the part with a turning ring. Tap the part, then the slot (drag also works in the real tool).
  3. Wrong move. The pointer tilts over the wrong slot (unsure) and the callout says why in one sentence. Nothing is undone for the student.
  4. Next control. Everything else dims and Kiki taps the Run button (tapping).
  5. Why. Kiki moves to the scope and asks a question (asking), which leads into the English explanation step.

Consumer provides: nothing for the demo version. In the app the same pattern is driven by the lab's known screen states and the fault cards. The callout is always attached to the pointer, one sentence, and the step name shows in the tool's title bar.

  • Do: let the app's own state decide where the pointer goes; Gemini's screenshot reading only narrates.
  • Don't: drag for the student after the demonstration. The second time, the student does it.

Language

LanguageDial

Five notches, student-controlled, Kiki suggests

The five-notch Odia-to-English slider that the student controls; Kiki can only suggest a notch.

Consumer provides: value (1 to 5) with onChange, or defaultValue; optional suggested (a notch: shown as a dashed ghost knob plus a "Try one notch more English?" chip) and onAcceptSuggestion.

Notches: 1 Odia with English terms, 2 mostly Odia, 3 half and half, 4 mostly English, 5 English with Odia on tap. Each notch change vibrates 10 ms on Android. Arrow keys, Home and End work on the knob.

  • Do: keep the dial in the lesson header at all times.
  • Don't: move the dial without the student. Never penalise a move toward Odia.

MorphText

The lesson paragraph that follows the dial

The lesson paragraph that re-renders at the student's dial level while the English term chips stay the same.

Consumer provides: level (1 to 5, from LanguageDial), levels (five arrays of segments: strings, or {term} objects for chips), optional glossary, termStates ({term: state}), onTermOpen. Odia runs are detected automatically and set 12% larger with a looser line height.

  • Do: generate all five levels for a card at once and cache them, so the morph is instant.
  • Don't: change which terms appear between levels: the chips are the anchors.

TermChip

Canonical English terms, tap for the Odia meaning

An English technical term inside running text, always in the same dotted-underline style; tapping opens a sheet with the Odia meaning, pronunciation and an example.

Consumer provides: term (the canonical English term, never translated), optional entry ({odia, example} from the glossary; defaults to the built-in sample glossary), state (new, collected, owned), pulse (a one-time ring when the paragraph morphs), onOpen.

  • Do: use one entry per term from the shared glossary so every lesson says the same thing.
  • Don't: style English terms any other way, or translate the term itself.

WordSticker

Collectible term cards that flip

A collectible card for one technical term that flips to show the Odia meaning and an example sentence.

Consumer provides: term, optional entry ({odia, example}), state (new: dashed edge, collected, owned: solid red once used correctly in English twice).

  • Do: reuse stickers as insertable chips in English answers.
  • Don't: show more than three new stickers in one Collect beat.

Progress

LessonProgress

Four-colour progress across a lesson

A four-segment bar at the top of the lesson player, one segment per mastery dimension in ring order.

Consumer provides: values ({concept, words, english, lab}, each 0 to 1).

  • Do: let it fill as beats complete so the student sees which skill grew.
  • Don't: use it for loading or time.

MapNode

Concepts as components on the breadboard

One concept on the breadboard map: a component with an LED, a small mastery ring and an optional past-paper heat badge.

Consumer provides: label, optional odia, state (locked, available, progress, mastered, flicker, or repair: a weak spot found by a practice set, drawn with a dashed body and an unlit LED), values for the ring, heat (such as "4/5" papers), here (shows Kiki as the you-are-here pin), onClick.

  • Do: draw prerequisites as wires; animate current only out of mastered nodes.
  • Don't: hide locked nodes: show them dashed so the path ahead is visible.

MasteryRing

Four segments: Concept, Words, English, Lab

A four-segment ring showing mastery of one concept: Concept (green), Words (red), English (yellow), Lab (blue), clockwise from the top.

Consumer provides: values ({concept, words, english, lab}, each 0 to 1, from rubric evidence only), optional size (44 on the map, 96 in the lesson header, 160+ on the receipt), locked (dimension keys drawn dashed, such as ["lab"] before the lab), flicker (time to revise), label, and children for the centre.

  • Do: fill segments only from real evidence; a full ring spins once and glows.
  • Don't: animate a segment to make someone feel good. Never show a ring without its four colours in this order.

ReceiptCompare

Before and after, the core proof of learning

The before-and-after pair at the start of the learning receipt: what the student said 10 minutes ago next to what they can say now.

Consumer provides: before and after ({time, answer, verdict?}).

  • Do: use the student's own words in both cards.
  • Don't: invent an "after" verdict: it comes from the rubric.

Learning

DiagnosisCard

Concept and English, judged separately

The result after an English answer, judging Concept and English separately so a language gap never hides real understanding.

Consumer provides: variant (solid, language, concept), optional title, message, actionLabel, onAction.

  • language: "You understand this. You just need the English words." Action: practise the words.
  • concept: reroute to a prerequisite. Action label "Rerouting…".
  • Do: show "not yet" as a dashed pencil outline. Don't use red or a cross: red means Words.

DiodeExplorable

Drag the voltage, watch current and the V-I curve

The worked-example interactive: drag the voltage across a silicon diode and watch current flow in the circuit and the point move along the V-I curve.

Consumer provides: optional defaultVoltage (volts, -2 to 1), id for the slider. The model is an ideal-ish silicon diode with the knee near 0.7 V; Kiki points when the voltage is near the knee.

This is the template for every explorable: one schematic, one slider, one live plot, one Kiki line. Build a new one per concept with the same parts.

VoiceScope

Hold to speak; your voice drawn as a waveform

Hold-to-speak recording shown as a live waveform on an oscilloscope screen, then playback, transcript and one fix.

Consumer provides: optional prompt (a sentence starter), transcript (node), feedback (one praise plus one fix), defaultState. The preview simulates audio; the app records with MediaRecorder and transcribes with Gemini.

  • Do: keep recordings at 30 s or less and play them back automatically.
  • Don't: grade pronunciation in the demo. Always offer typing as a fallback.

Lab

FaultCard

The debug challenge, for any course

The debug challenge card: the fault type, the visible symptom, Kiki's "why" questions one at a time, and the fixed state.

Consumer provides: type (one of the seven fault types: Flipped, Wrong value, Missing piece, Wrong connection, Wrong tool setting, Wrong measurement, Wrong assumption), symptom, questions (three, open to specific), optional fixed, fixedMessage, onFixed.

  • Do: choose the fault card from the student's weakest misconception.
  • Don't: give the fix before the third question.

LabStepper

Predict, act, observe, explain, debug

The lab's Predict, Act, Observe, Explain, Debug stepper with Kiki's current instruction card.

Consumer provides: current (0 to 4), optional steps, title, hint, kikiState, onNext, nextLabel.

  • Do: keep instructions to one action each.
  • Don't: skip Predict or Explain in the flow: they produce the evidence.

PredictionCanvas

Draw your prediction, then run

A dark scope screen where the student sketches the output they expect before running the simulation; the real trace is then drawn over the sketch with a short verdict.

Consumer provides: expected (halfwave, fullwave, sine, or a function from 0..1 to -1..1), optional onResult (receives a 0 to 1 similarity score).

  • Do: always show the input faintly so the student has a reference.
  • Don't: reveal the real output before the student has drawn or chosen to skip.

Spotlight

Dim everything except the control Kiki means

Dims a lab tool's interface except one target control, which gets a pulsing blue ring; used by Kiki's copilot and by the software tour.

Consumer provides: children laid out as the tool; wrap the target in Spotlight.Target. Optional active (false removes the dim) and style.

  • Do: spotlight one control at a time.
  • Don't: spotlight a control Kiki is not confident about: switch Kiki to unsure and offer the known-state picker instead.

Exam

AnswerOverlay

Snap your answer: concept in green, English in yellow

Snap your answer: the student's handwritten exam answer marked with green ticks for the concept criteria and yellow underlines where the English cost marks; tapping a mark shows the Odia explanation and exam-ready English.

Consumer provides: data ({question, score: {concept, english}, lines: [{tick: {label, ok}, parts: [string | {issue, text}]}], issues: [{kind: "mark" | "tip", odia, fix, cost}]}). In the app the photo is the background; this component draws a ruled-paper mock in the preview. The paper stays light in dark theme on purpose, like a real sheet.

  • Do: separate marks lost to English (wavy yellow) from grammar tips that cost nothing (dotted).
  • Don't: show false precision: use a mark range when Gemini is unsure.

PracticeReport

Analysis of a written practice set

The analysis after a written practice set: the score, how many marks were lost to English and how many to concept gaps, each question with its own split, and the weak spots to fix before the exam.

Consumer provides: data ({title, time, total, questions: [{n, topic, got, max, english, note}]}, where english is the marks lost only because of English), onOpen(question) to open that answer in AnswerOverlay, onRepair for "Make my repair map" (pass false to hide it).

Concept marks lost are worked out as max − got − english. A question is a weak spot when it lost 2 or more marks to the concept, or any marks to English.

  • Do: show the English cost separately every time. It is the core insight for the student.
  • Do: open each question's marked-up answer on tap.
  • Don't: show a rank or compare with classmates.

Feedback

Snackbar

Short status messages

A short dark status message at the bottom of the screen, such as "Rerouting… +1 stop, 6 min" or "No signal. Your progress is saved on this phone."

Consumer provides: message, optional tone (route: a blue route-line mark), icon, actionLabel with onAction.

  • Do: say what happened and what it means for the student.
  • Don't: show error codes or apologise.

SourceTag

Where a lesson card came from

A chip on a lesson card naming where its content came from, such as "From your notes, page 7"; tapping shows the snippet and any conflict with the textbook.

Consumer provides: label, source (file name), snippet, optional conflict (one sentence telling the student which value to use in the exam).

  • Do: show the student's own material first; it is the first source of truth.

Teachers

ClassPulseBar

Mastered, language gap, concept gap per concept

For teachers: one concept's class split into mastered, language gap and concept gap, with the numbers in words beside the bar.

Consumer provides: label, mastered, language, concept (percentages), optional students, hidden (true when fewer than 10 students tried it).

  • Do: show class totals only.
  • Don't: link to individual students' answers unless the student shared them.

Kiki artwork

Kiki's guide artwork: Kiki as a companion cursor that lives beside the student's own cursor or finger, flies to the thing that matters on their screen, and shows them the route one step at a time. Use these for slides, the pitch deck, specs and anywhere the live KikiPointer can't run.

The guide grammar (every scene follows it):

  • Step now: a halo on the target and a filled number badge.
  • Steps ahead: ghost (dashed) number badges joined by a dashed route that flows towards them. The student sees steps 2 and 3 while doing step 1.
  • Done: the route behind turns solid and the badge becomes a tick.
  • Where Kiki came from: the four dots trail behind the pointer along its flight path. A faint dotted line shows a longer flight, for example from beside the student's cursor.
  • Kiki's eyes look at the next thing, not at the student, so the gaze itself points the way.
  • Kiki never covers the target. It parks at the edge of the halo, and its marks run beside a wire or a line of text (a rail), never on top of the student's diagram.
  • Colour is the skill: green for an idea, red for a technical term, yellow for exam English, blue in the lab. Red never means wrong.

Files (each scene is 320 × 220 and uses the same worked example: R3 in series, then R1 and R2 in parallel):

FileMoveUse it when Kiki…
kiki-guide-look.svgLook hereflies from beside the student's cursor to the first thing to look at
kiki-guide-path-ahead.svgPath aheadhas started step 1 and shows steps 2 and 3 waiting on the route
kiki-guide-trace.svgTracerides along a wire or path (current, flow, a sequence), solid behind and dashed ahead
kiki-guide-connect.svgConnectlinks two parts and names what they share
kiki-guide-your-turn.svgYour turnhands the next step to the student and waits beside the target
kiki-guide-redirect.svgRedirectdraws the way from where the student tapped to where they should look ("Close. Look here instead")
kiki-guide-show-me.svgShow medemonstrates a drag in the lab, from the parts tray to the slot
kiki-guide-ask.svgAskasks a question and waits between the answers
kiki-guide-done.svgDonemarks the route complete: every step ticked, a small hop
kiki-guide-words.svgWordsuses the same grammar on text: sweeps the term, shows the next phrase ahead
kiki-guide-thinking.svgThinkingis reading the student's screen (Gemini at work)
kiki-guide-listening.svgListeningis recording the student's voice
kiki-guide-unsure.svgUnsureis not sure which part the student means, so it offers the candidates instead of guessing
kiki-guide-storyboard.svgStoryboardthe series-or-parallel question guided in four moves: look, path ahead, connect, your turn
kiki-pointer.svgPointerthe bare pointer with its trail, for avatars and small marks (160 × 160)

Scenes animate gently where a browser shows them through an <img> (the halo pulses, the route ahead flows, the wait ring turns). A static copy shows the first frame, which is complete on its own.

Inks: the pointer body is #1f1f1f with a #ffffff outline, white eyes with dark pupils, in every theme. The dots are always blue #4285f4, red #ea4335, yellow #fbbc05 and green #34a853, in that order: they are Kiki's identity, not the skill colours. Source: design-system/tools/build-kiki.js regenerates every file.
